deep.reconstruction:
PART 1 – 'Zur Variationsrechnung' (Fermat's principle for a ray in an inhomogeneous medium).

Problem: make J = ∫ n(x,y) ds = ∫ n √(1+p²) dx stationary, with p = dy/dx and ds = √(dx²+dy²). The context is terrestrial refraction: the previous page ends with refraction coefficients from the 1821–23 triangulation. So n is the refractive index and the curve is a light ray.

Notation: Gauss writes p = tan φ, so φ is the inclination of the tangent to the x-axis, cos φ = 1/√(1+p²) and sin φ = p/√(1+p²). Only y is varied (δx = 0).

Step 1 (first variation): δJ = ∫ { dx·n_y·√(1+p²)·δy + n p/√(1+p²) · d(δy) }, using δp·dx = d(δy).

Step 2 (trigonometric rewrite): δJ = ∫ { dx·n_y·δy/cos φ + n sin φ · d(δy) }.

Step 3 (integration by parts): δJ = n sin φ δy + ∫ { dx·n_y·δy/cos φ − δy·d(n sin φ) }.
- Here d(n sin φ) = n cos φ dφ + sin φ (n_x dx + n_y dy).
- This gives exactly the four terms on the page: ∫(dx n_y δy/cos φ − n cos φ dφ δy − sin φ δy n_x dx − sin φ δy n_y dy).

Step 4 [implicit step, mine: substitute dy = tan φ dx]: δJ = n sin φ δy + ∫ dx δy { n_y/cos φ − n cos φ φ_x − n_x sin φ − n_y sin²φ/cos φ }.
- Since 1/cos φ − sin²φ/cos φ = cos φ, this is n sin φ δy + ∫ dx δy { n_y cos φ − n_x sin φ − n cos φ dφ/dx }.

Step 5 (condition for the extremum): the bracket must vanish, i.e. n_y cos φ − n_x sin φ = n cos φ dφ/dx = n dφ/ds, because ds = dx/cos φ.

Modern form: the ray curvature is κ = dφ/ds = ∇(ln n)·N, with unit normal N = (−sin φ, cos φ). The ray bends toward increasing index. This is the ray (eikonal) equation that underlies the theory of atmospheric refraction.

PART 2 – Circle through three points (plane geometry for station/resection work).

Setup: A, B, C are points in a plane; f, g, h are the azimuths of AB, AC, BC.

Claim (i): f+g−h is the azimuth at A of the tangent to the circle through A, B, C. The tangent is oriented so that it runs around the circle in the same sense as BC runs around the triangle.
- Reason [mine]: by the tangent–chord (alternate segment) theorem, the tangent at A is antiparallel to BC with respect to the angle at A.
- Equivalently, its direction is the reflection of direction h in the bisector (f+g)/2, i.e. f+g−h.
- This formula is independent of whether azimuths are counted clockwise or counterclockwise.

Claim (ii): radius R = BC/(2 sin(g−f)). This is the law of sines, since the angle at A is g−f (signed, which also encodes orientation).

Claim (iii): let P lie from A at azimuth f+g−h+φ (angle φ from the tangent) and at distance BC sin φ / sin(g−f) = 2R sin φ.
- That is precisely the chord of the circle making angle φ with the tangent, so P lies on the circumcircle.
- By the inscribed-angle theorem, the angle BPC equals the angle BAC.
- This parametrizes the locus of points seeing BC under the same angle (the circle used in the Snellius–Pothenot resection problem).
errors: No substantive errors in the variational computation. Each step checks, including the simplification n_y/cosφ − n_y sin²φ/cosφ = n_y cosφ and dφ/dx·cosφ = dφ/ds.
The boundary term n sinφ δy is simply carried along. Fixed endpoints (δy = 0 at the ends) are tacitly assumed, as is only the variation of y with x as the independent variable. Both are standard.

Part 2(iii): 'the angle between B and C is the same as at A' holds as an oriented angle between lines (mod 180°). If P falls on the arc BC not containing A, the ordinary angle BPC is the supplement 180° − A. This is a minor unstated caveat.

results.what: Euler–Lagrange equation for ∫ n ds giving ray curvature dφ/ds = (n_y cosφ − n_x sinφ)/n
results.modern_name: Fermat's principle / ray (eikonal) equation in a medium of variable refractive index; curvature of a light ray equals the normal derivative of ln n
results.usually_credited_to: Fermat (principle, 1662); variational form Euler/Lagrange (1744–1760s); refraction-ray curvature formulas Bouguer, Laplace (Mécanique céleste, Book X, 1805)

results.what: Azimuth of the circumcircle tangent at A equals f+g−h (tangent antiparallel to BC)
results.modern_name: Tangent–chord (alternate segment) theorem expressed in azimuths

results.what: Circumradius R = BC/(2 sin A) and point P at azimuth tangent+φ, distance 2R sinφ lies on the circle, seeing BC under the same angle
results.modern_name: Law of sines / inscribed angle theorem; locus circle of the Snellius–Pothenot resection problem
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (Euclid III.21; Snellius 1617, Pothenot 1692 for resection)

deep.surprise_reason: Both parts are routine. The variational derivation of the ray equation was standard from Euler/Lagrange and Laplace's refraction theory. Gauss's interest in terrestrial refraction during the Hanover triangulation is well documented. The circle facts are classical geometry phrased in azimuths for geodetic use. The only interest is the clean trigonometric (tangent-angle φ) form and the azimuth formula f+g−h as a working tool.

transcription_corrections: The variation symbols are δ (variation) and ∂ (differential) as in the image: 'n sinφ.δy', '∂δy' = d(δy). The machine transcription is essentially faithful.
Line 3 of the derivation reads '− sinφ.δy(∂n/∂x)∂x − sinφ.δy(∂n/∂y)∂y' in the image; this is correct as transcribed.

In the second part the manuscript reads 'die Richtung, welche in demselben Sinn um die Kreisfläche läuft, wie BC um das Dreieck' and 'so ist in P der Winkel zwischen B und C derselbe wie in A'. The transcription agrees. The marginal letters near these lines are sheet/marker annotations, not mathematics.
